name: Leveling and Sharpening
description: As stories are retold, some details are flattened or dropped ('leveling') while a few striking or schema-fitting details get exaggerated ('sharpening'). Repetition does not preserve memory neutrally; it edits it.
design_relevance_note: Very limited direct interface relevance. Its main value is as a warning about retold research findings, stakeholder handoffs, community rumors, and repeated incident narratives becoming simpler in some places and overstated in others over time.
myth_risk_note: Leveling and sharpening are not mainstream constructs in contemporary behavioral-economics or choice-architecture literature -- the only genuinely on-topic paper found is the original 1954 Holzman & Klein study, with no modern peer-reviewed follow-up located in this pass (a near-total homonym collision, with most candidates being unrelated physical-science literature). The concept has real historical roots (Bartlett's serial-reproduction paradigm predates it) but its application to contemporary design/decision-making practice is thin and under-theorized relative to other memory-distortion phenomena in this taxonomy.
prevalence_note: Mostly an older academic memory/rumor term with occasional relevance to research communication, not a mainstream named concept in ordinary digital-product design.

findings.description: Holzman and Gardner treated leveling and sharpening as systematic aspects of memory organization, with remembered material becoming compressed in some respects and selectively accentuated in others rather than reproduced verbatim.
findings.source_venue: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
